plate_findings.evidence: Fundoscopic exam of the right eye demonstrates anomalous optic nerves with multiple cilioretinal vessels

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Right-eye fundus photograph from a papillorenal syndrome case shows the disease-attributable anomalous optic disc with cilioretinal vessels; Elschnig-type spots are considered coexisting hypertensive retinopathy and are not used for papillorenal attribution. B: Left-eye fundus photograph from the same papillorenal syndrome case shows an anomalous optic disc with cilioretinal vessels; hypopigmented Elschnig-like lesions are not attributed to papillorenal syndrome.
panels.attribution_text: Ali et al. De Novo PAX2 Mutation With Associated Papillorenal Syndrome: A Case Report and Literature Review of Penetrance and Expressivity.. Cureus 2022. doi:10.7759/cureus.29026. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Fundoscopic exam of the right (A) and left (B) eye at initial presentation demonstrates anomalous optic nerves with multiple cilioretinal vessels (black arrows) and trace peri-papillary atrophy as well as bilateral hypopigmented lesions, suggestive of Elschnig spots (white arrows).
in_text_mentions: ysis-dependent end-stage renal disease (ESRD) and hypertension. She also had a known history of hypertensive retinopathy. On presentation, her visual acuity (VA) was 20/20 in both eyes. Intraocular pressure was 16 mmHg in both eyes. Anterior segment examination was unremarkable. Dilated eye exam revealed macular retinal pigment epithelial changes, Siegrist lines, and Elschnig spots in both eyes (Figure 1). Humphrey visual fields (HVF) (Humphrey Visual Field Analyzer II-I, Carl Zeiss Meditec, Inc. Dublin, CA) showed good reliability and revealed enlarged blind spots bilaterally (Figure 2A, 2B).

plate_findings.evidence: caption: retinal pigment epithelial changes in the right eye

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Infrared fundus photo from a papillorenal syndrome case report; caption documents retinal pigment epithelial changes and subretinal drusenoid deposits in the right eye. These retinal findings are atypical for the syndrome compared with classic optic disc anomalies, but are the specific captioned patient manifestation. B: Infrared fundus photo from the same papillorenal syndrome case report; caption states subretinal drusenoid deposits are bilateral (white arrows). No directly matching term appears in the provided vocabulary, so the visible/captioned finding is recorded as a proposed finding.

plate_findings.evidence: fetal kidneys not well visualized due to low amniotic fluid; severe oligohydramnios at 16 weeks in fetus later diagnosed with RCS

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Antenatal ultrasound of fetus with renal coloboma syndrome showing severe oligohydramnios, an early prenatal presentation; renal findings not clearly visible. B: Repeat antenatal ultrasound at 36 weeks in the same RCS pregnancy showing resolution of oligohydramnios; no specific morphologic abnormality visible.
panels.attribution_text: Nguyen et al. Resolving severe oligohydramnios as an early prenatal presentation of renal coloboma syndrome-A report of two generations.. Clinical case reports 2021. doi:10.1002/ccr3.4758. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: A, Antenatal ultrasound image at 16 weeks and 1 day gestation showing a transverse view of the uterus with severe oligohydramnios. B, Antenatal ultrasound image at 36 weeks gestation showing normal amniotic fluid with a maximum vertical pocket of 6.89 cm
in_text_mentions: d to the Maternal Fetal Medicine (MFM) clinic given a personal history of obesity and chronic renal disease post‐transplant. She was seen at 16 weeks and 1 day gestation with findings of severe oligohydramnios on a viability US. (Figure 1A). A limited survey of the anatomy was attempted during which the bladder and fetal kidneys were not well visualized due to the low amniotic fluid, large maternal body habitus, and the early gestational age. The patient denied any symptoms of vaginal fluid loss and had no known exposure to teratogens or any relevant medications (eg, NSAIDs or ACE inhibitors).

The timing of the results coincided with a repeat US at 36 weeks in which amniotic fluid levels normalized (Figure 1B). Around that time, our patient started experiencing abnormal vision in the context of a headache. Recognizing the ocular spectrum of RCS, this prompted an urgent ocular assessment. Dilated fundus examination of both eyes revealed no retinal tears or detachments. No ocular coloboma was observed; however, there was vitreous syneresis and dilated vessels in the right eye.
